displayQuote: For some people, four walls are three too many

meta.title: Who really said "For some people, four walls are three too many"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No evidence Stalin said it. Wikiquote lists the line as misattributed; it seems to adapt a prison remark credited to Spanish royalist Domingo de Monteverde.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'For some people, four walls are three too many'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Stalin. Wikiquote calls it misattributed and traces it to a remark credited to Domingo de Monteverde: four walls are three too many for a prison.

answer.label: Not Joseph Stalin — apparently adapted from a remark credited to Domingo de Monteverde
answer.authorDates: 1773–1832 · Spanish soldier, Captain General of Venezuela 1812–1813
answer.sourceLine: Nothing documented links this line to Stalin. Wikiquote lists it as misattributed and says it “seems to have originated” with Monteverde. Karen Racine’s Francisco de Miranda (2003), p. 239, quotes him as saying that “four walls are three too many for a prison — you only need one for an execution.” The popular wording cuts out the prison and the execution.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life in the Age of Revolution
p. 239 (as cited by Wikiquote; not inspected by Quotle.info)

source.excerpt: “four walls are three too many for a prison — you only need one for an execution.”
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists “For some people, four walls are three too many” in the Misattributed section of its Joseph Stalin page. It says the line “seems to have originated” with Juan Domingo de Monteverde and cites Racine’s 2003 book, p. 239.
Quote aggregators still post the line under Stalin. Quotepark ↗ files it under his name but marks it misattributed, repeating Wikiquote’s Monteverde note.
The cited book is real. A review in The Americas ↗ gives it as Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life in the Age of Revolution (Wilmington: Scholarly Resources, 2003).
For context, Wikipedia ↗ records that Monteverde led the royalist campaign against Miranda’s First Republic of Venezuela in 1812, and that Miranda was imprisoned after the capitulation.
source.excerptNote: The remark credited to Monteverde, in the wording Wikiquote gives from Racine’s book. Quotle.info could not find a scan or preview of p. 239 to check this against. The popular “Stalin” version keeps only the first clause and drops “for a prison.”
source.rightsNote: The popular “Stalin” wording has no identifiable source, so no rights status is claimed for it. The fuller Monteverde wording is quoted from Karen Racine’s 2003 biography, a modern in-copyright book. Whether that English rendering is Racine’s own translation was not verified.

author.name: Domingo de Monteverde
author.heading: About the probable source
author.metaLine: 1773–1832 · Spanish soldier and Captain General of Venezuela
author.bio: Juan Domingo de Monteverde was a Spanish officer born in Tenerife. He led the royalist campaign that brought down the First Republic of Venezuela in 1812, and he served as Captain General of Venezuela from June 1812 until Simón Bolívar defeated him in 1813. Karen Racine’s biography of his opponent, Francisco de Miranda, quotes him with the prison remark that the “Stalin” line appears to shorten (as reported by Wikiquote).

cite.sourceCitation: Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life in the Age of Revolution (Wilmington: Scholarly Resources, 2003), 239, quoting Domingo de Monteverde, as reported in Wikiquote, “Joseph Stalin,” Misattributed section. No documented source attributes the popular wording to Stalin.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Stalin
misattribution.intro: The line circulates online as a Stalin quip. No speech, letter or document by Stalin contains it, and the specialist sources that have looked at it say it is misattributed.

items.why: No source in Stalin’s works or recorded remarks is ever cited for the line. Wikiquote ↗ lists it as misattributed, and aggregators such as Quotepark ↗ carry the same label.

According to Wikiquote ↗, Racine’s Francisco de Miranda (2003), p. 239, quotes the Spanish royalist commander as saying “four walls are three too many for a prison — you only need one for an execution.”

misattribution.truthLine: Stalin is not known to have said this. In the account given by Wikiquote ↗, the line is a shortened form of a remark about prisons and executions that Karen Racine’s 2003 biography of Miranda credits to Domingo de Monteverde.

context.heading: What got lost in the retelling
lead: The remark credited to Monteverde is a threat: a prisoner needs only one wall, the one he is shot against. The viral version drops “for a prison” and “execution,” so the threat reads like a dry comment about people who can’t stand being confined.

Our own reading of why it lands on Stalin: a grim one-liner about walls and executions fits his reputation, and he already draws invented quotes. The same Wikiquote section also debunks the better-known “one death is a tragedy, a million deaths is a statistic.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists 'For some people, four walls are three too many' under Stalin's Misattributed section, saying it seems to have originated with Juan Domingo de Monteverde, quoted in Racine (2003) p. 239 as 'four walls are three too many for a prison — you only need one for an execution.'
Quotepark files the line under Joseph Stalin, marks it misattributed and repeats the Monteverde/Racine note (adapted from Wikiquote).
Karen Racine, Francisco de Miranda: A Transatlantic Life in the Age of Revolution, Wilmington: Scholarly Resources, 2003, xix+336 pp. (reviewed in The Americas 60:3, 2004).

Monteverde (2 April 1773 – 15 September 1832), born in San Cristóbal de La Laguna, Tenerife, was Captain General of Venezuela June 1812 – August 1813, led the campaign that ended the First Republic in 1812, and was defeated by Bolívar in 1813; Miranda was imprisoned after the 1812 capitulation.
